Yes. If both were considered murder, you'd be charged with two counts of murder instead of one... So this point falls short of explaining the rationale well.

The real reason is the same as why we have different "degrees" of murder, as well as manslaughter and homicide. There's different charges because there are different circumstances and situations... And attempted murder has a different outcome.

If you accidentally run over your daughter with a car (maybe while she sunbathes in the driveway -- it's happened, so this isn't too far fetched) and kill her, you would get a different sentence than if you did the same with cruel and malicious intent.

So, in a way, OP answered his own question. Yes, if you rob a bank, you'll get charged regardless of if you succeed or not. And if you try to kill someone, you'll get charged regardless of if you succeed or not. But, since we have more lenient sentencing for the varying degrees of murder, and even separate categories (that aren't murder) for killing people, we ultimately have a lighter charge for not succeeding, the same way we have a lighter charge for if you accidentally run your daughter over.
